Apply controls across both the BlueHammer exploit path and the credential-reuse activity that may follow.

Update Microsoft Defender. Run Defender Antimalware Platform version 4.18.26030.3011 or later to close the vulnerable path used by CVE-2026-33825.

Restrict privileged domain logons on workstations. Use administrative tiering and privileged-access workstations to keep reusable domain-administrator credentials off lower-trust endpoints. Use Remote Credential Guard where supported.

Enforce WDAC or AppLocker. A properly scoped allowlist can block the unsigned PoC and similar unapproved executables before execution.

Enable Credential Guard and LSA Protection. Credential Guard isolates many NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets, while LSA Protection restricts untrusted code from loading into LSASS. Because these controls do not cover every credential type or logon scenario, privileged logon restrictions remain necessary.

Deploy Windows LAPS. Unique, automatically rotated local-administrator passwords limit credential reuse between endpoints. LAPS do not prevent LSASS access or domain-credential theft after a SYSTEM compromise.

Together, these controls reduce the risk of credential theft and lateral movement, although they do not eliminate the impact of a local SYSTEM compromise.

Conclusion

BlueHammer chains legitimate Windows mechanisms including a CloudFilter callback, batch oplock, object-manager symlink, Defender update RPC interface, offline SAM parsing, and SAMR operations to achieve local privilege escalation. In our tests, the chain produced a SYSTEM shell on an affected Defender platform when the required conditions, including a pending signature update, were present.

The vulnerability itself is limited to local privilege escalation. Its enterprise impact can extend beyond the compromised endpoint when privileged credentials are present. In our lab, credential material recovered from the SYSTEM shell was reused to authenticate to the domain controller.

Microsoft lists Defender Antimalware Platform version 4.18.26030.3011 as the fixed boundary for CVE-2026-33825. Defenders should update affected endpoints, identify systems where the exploit prerequisites are present, and correlate CloudFilter, oplock, RPC, symlink, SAMR, password-change, and service-creation activity. TruConfirm strengthens this assessment by safely validating the critical exploit primitive without executing the destructive stages of the original PoC.

References
  • Microsoft Security Update Guide — CVE-2026-33825
  • NVD — CVE-2026-33825
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is BlueHammer?

An eight-stage local privilege-escalation chain against Windows Defender, tracked as CVE-2026-33825. It needs standard-user code execution first. It does not provide initial access.

Which Defender versions are affected?

Microsoft lists Antimalware Platform versions earlier than 4.18.26030.3011. Version 4.18.26030.3011 and later close the vulnerable path.

Does TruConfirm run the full exploit?

No. It checks environmental preconditions and safely validates the CloudFilter freeze. It does not extract SAM, reset passwords, create a service, recover credentials, or spawn a SYSTEM shell.

Can BlueHammer become a domain admin by itself?

No. The vulnerability is local privilege escalation. Domain impact requires reusable privileged credentials already present on the endpoint that the SYSTEM shell can access.

What are the highest-signal IoCs?

On the analyzed PoC: the strings IHATEMICROSOFT and $PWNed666!!!WDFAIL, two FSCTL 0x90008 batch oplocks in one binary, and unexpected RPC to MpAmDefinitionUpdateAPI (UUID c503f532-443a-4c69-8300-ccd1fbdb3839). Static strings can be removed in modified builds; correlate behavioral signals.

items.title: Google Public Sector increases partner investments for frontline adoption
How Commerce.com and Cloudflare are getting storefronts ready for AI agents
items.summary: AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online. That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it. Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like search_products . Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, it’s currently available behind experimental Chrome flags ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like Cloudflare Kitesurf . In August, we launched edge implementation of WebMCP in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code. Commerce.com , a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. So when the preview came out, they asked: Can we turn this on for all of our stores at once? Here’s why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP, how we built edge-level opt-outs to give every merchant control, and what we learned along the way. Why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP Kristina Pototska, Product Management Director at Commerce.com, explains why this matters for storefronts: “Merchants keep asking us how they can keep up with agentic shopping. When a shopper asks an agent to find something, merchants want their store to be in the answer. They want to keep the customer, keep control of the checkout, and do it without rebuilding their site. WebMCP helps with all three. The agent gets real tools to search products, check details, build a cart, and get a checkout link, so it doesn’t have to guess its way around the page. The human shopper stays on the merchant’s site, and the merchant keeps the relationship. We wanted to turn this on in a secure way, and without asking merchants to edit their theme or do anything by hand. That’s where the Cloudflare partnership worked perfectly. WebMCP also works side by side with our server-side MCP , and together they cover the different ways people shop with agents. Server-side MCP supports agents that connect to a store directly, like an assistant helping someone shop across several sites. WebMCP supports agents that work in the shopper’s browser. It’s the same set of shopping tools in both cases, so merchants don’t have to choose between the two or manage them separately.” Under the hood, this integration relies on two key principles. First, the WebMCP tools execute directly inside the shopper's active browser session on the storefront's domain, ensuring the agent sees the same prices and cart. No credentials go to a third party, and the visit still happens on the merchant's site. Second, Cloudflare serves as the edge delivery layer for Commerce.com’s backend MCP server, proxying tool definitions and actions unchanged so merchants maintain full control over their tool logic. What a shopper's agent sees When visiting an enabled Commerce.com storefront, an AI assistant no longer has to guess how to navigate the site. Instead, it can instantly discover tools via WebMCP. Suppose you tell your agent: "Find me a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 and add it to my cart." Without WebMCP: The agent attempts to simulate human clicks, only to get blocked by cookie banners, misinterpret variant drop-downs, or get tripped up by bot challenges that try to distinguish automated traffic from real customers. items.summary_html:
AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online.

That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it.

Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like search_products. Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, it’s currently available behind experimental Chrome flags (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like Cloudflare Kitesurf.

In August, we launched edge implementation of WebMCP in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code.

Commerce.com, a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. So when the preview came out, they asked: Can we turn this on for all of our stores at once?

Here’s why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP, how we built edge-level opt-outs to give every merchant control, and what we learned along the way.

Why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP

Kristina Pototska, Product Management Director at Commerce.com, explains why this matters for storefronts:

“Merchants keep asking us how they can keep up with agentic shopping. When a shopper asks an agent to find something, merchants want their store to be in the answer. They want to keep the customer, keep control of the checkout, and do it without rebuilding their site. WebMCP helps with all three. The agent gets real tools to search products, check details, build a cart, and get a checkout link, so it doesn’t have to guess its way around the page. The human shopper stays on the merchant’s site, and the merchant keeps the relationship.
We wanted to turn this on in a secure way, and without asking merchants to edit their theme or do anything by hand. That’s where the Cloudflare partnership worked perfectly.
WebMCP also works side by side with our server-side MCP, and together they cover the different ways people shop with agents. Server-side MCP supports agents that connect to a store directly, like an assistant helping someone shop across several sites. WebMCP supports agents that work in the shopper’s browser. It’s the same set of shopping tools in both cases, so merchants don’t have to choose between the two or manage them separately.”

Under the hood, this integration relies on two key principles. First, the WebMCP tools execute directly inside the shopper's active browser session on the storefront's domain, ensuring the agent sees the same prices and cart. No credentials go to a third party, and the visit still happens on the merchant's site. Second, Cloudflare serves as the edge delivery layer for Commerce.com’s backend MCP server, proxying tool definitions and actions unchanged so merchants maintain full control over their tool logic.

What a shopper's agent sees

When visiting an enabled Commerce.com storefront, an AI assistant no longer has to guess how to navigate the site. Instead, it can instantly discover tools via WebMCP.

Suppose you tell your agent: "Find me a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 and add it to my cart."

Without WebMCP: The agent attempts to simulate human clicks, only to get blocked by cookie banners, misinterpret variant drop-downs, or get tripped up by bot challenges that try to distinguish automated traffic from real customers.

With WebMCP: The agent detects the store's tools on document.modelContext and makes two clean calls:

  1. search_products({ query: "trail running shoe", max_price: 140, size: 10 })
  2. add_to_cart({ product_id: "shoe_123" })

Because the agent runs inside your active browser session on the store's domain, your cart updates in real time. Commerce.com’s backend MCP server determines the commerce flow: when you’re ready to complete the purchase, you click checkout yourself — keeping your payment details secure and leaving you in complete control of the final buy.

What we built together

When Commerce.com asked to turn on WebMCP across almost 100000 storefronts, we ran into a practical challenge: WebMCP was originally designed as a single on-or-off switch for an entire domain zone.

Commerce wanted to enable our mcp-server-client toolpack, which acts as an edge bridge — proxying tool definitions and requests directly from Commerce.com’s backend MCP server to the visitor's browser. Because Commerce.com uses Cloudflare for SaaS to host thousands of merchant vanity domains on shared zones, we needed a way to deliver this platform-wide while giving individual store owners an easy way to opt out.

1. On for all stores on Commerce.com, with an opt-out for each merchant

Instead of building a complex custom allowlist, we hooked WebMCP into the existing Cloudflare concepts of Configuration Rules and custom hostname metadata.

Commerce.com turns WebMCP on for their main zone, then adds a rule at the edge that checks merchant metadata. If a merchant flips the "opt-out" switch in their Commerce.com dashboard, Cloudflare bypasses WebMCP for that specific storefront automatically:

{
  "action": "set_config",
  "expression": "cf.hostname.metadata.webmcp_opt_out eq \"true\"",
  "action_parameters": {
    "webmcp_enabled": false
  }
}

Because Cloudflare evaluates these rules at the edge before serving the page, an opted-out store gets zero extra latency, no remote lookups, and no injected scripts.

2. Tailored endpoints and safe fallbacks

As with any preview release, working with a partner in the real world revealed a few practical details we hadn't accounted for:

Custom MCP paths: When the mcp-server-client toolpack was enabled, our bridge originally expected to find every site's MCP server at /mcp. Commerce.com’s server lives at /api/mcp. To handle this, we added a configurable MCP URL setting at the zone level. When this is set, we pass the custom path into the injected script tag:

Seamless fallbacks: If a store's MCP server is offline or a customer's browser doesn't support WebMCP, the script exits. The storefront loads normally and human shoppers aren't affected.

What's next

We'll keep investing in WebMCP as the standard evolves, starting with helping agents find a site's tools more easily. Cloudflare and Commerce.com will continue to work together to make shopping with agents fast, reliable and safe for both merchants and shoppers.

If you're at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco on October 21, 2026, come see us at Getting your storefront agent ready for peak season, a panel discussion featuring Kristina Pototska (Product Management Director, Commerce), Justis Blasco (CTO and Co-Founder, Popmenu), Ross Harvey (Head of Infrastructure, Fruugo), and Josh Mills (VP of Engineering, Gopuff).

items.summary: What Is Log Analytics? Log analytics is the practice of collecting, parsing, normalizing, and querying machine-generated event records to answer an operational or security question. In a SOC, that question is usually narrow: did this account authenticate from an unexpected source, did this host spawn an unusual child process, which API calls preceded the data transfer. The raw material is heterogeneous: Windows Security and Sysmon channels in .evtx files, Linux auth.log and journald output, firewall and proxy events in CEF, and cloud audit trails such as AWS CloudTrail or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs exported as JSON. A working log analytics pipeline has four stages: Collection. Export events from the source without losing fields or timestamps. Normalization. Map src_ip, IpAddress, and sourceIPAddress to one common schema. Detection. Run Sigma or vendor rules and tag every hit with MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Correlation. Group related hits into a timeline or attack chain that an analyst can validate. Why Log Analytics Matters for Detection and Response Logs are often the only record that survives an intrusion. EDR telemetry rolls over, memory is lost on reboot, and packet capture is rarely running when you need it. Windows Event IDs 4624, 4672, and 4688, or CloudTrail calls such as ConsoleLogin and CreateAccessKey, are typically the primary evidence for scoping an incident. Three pressures make log analytics a core SOC skill rather than a SIEM feature: Volume. A single incident can produce millions of events, and grep only finds what you already know to look for. Coverage gaps. Contractor laptops, OT segments, and SaaS tenants nobody connected are not in the SIEM, but their logs still need analysis. Data handling. Logs carry usernames, hostnames, IPs, session cookies, and bearer tokens. Under GDPR much of that is personal data, and a leaked token is a live access path. Every log attached to a vendor ticket or pasted into an AI chat widens the circle of people and jurisdictions that can read the original values. Good log analytics answers the question fast without creating a second incident. A Short History of Log Analytics Syslog, written by Eric Allman for Sendmail in the early 1980s, was later standardized in RFC 3164 (2001) and RFC 5424 (2009). For two decades, log analysis meant grep and awk on a central syslog server. Windows went structured. Windows Vista replaced the legacy .evt format with the XML-based .evtx format and the channel model still used today, and Sysmon (2014) added high-fidelity process and network telemetry. The mid-2000s brought SIEM. ArcSight, QRadar, and later Splunk made centralized search and correlation a product category, and ArcSight’s CEF is still emitted by most network appliances. The 2010s added open stacks such as ELK and cloud audit trails such as CloudTrail (2013). In 2017, Sigma gave defenders a vendor-neutral rule format. The same year, SOC Prime began tagging Sigma rules with MITRE ATT&CK techniques and applied the approach to the public NotPetya investigation. ATT&CK mapping has since become a default expectation for detection content. Where Log Analytics Is Heading Detection moves upstream. Teams run Sigma rules on streaming events in the pipeline before data reaches the SIEM, cutting storage cost and shrinking mean time to detect from hours to minutes. Correlation beats single alerts. Isolated low-fidelity matches are noise. Higher-order logic that links techniques across hosts and time windows into attack chains gives analysts something to confirm or close. AI triage meets data-handling limits. LLMs explain process trees and summarize timelines well, but sending raw telemetry to a model provider raises privacy and contractual questions, and frontier models may refuse security content outright. During the July 2026 HuggingFace incident response, an attempt to send about 17,000 events to frontier models was blocked by guardrails. Pseudonymization becomes a pipeline stage. Static masking destroys correlation, and plain hashes can be reversed by dictionary guessing. Keyed HMAC tokens keep relationships intact while removing the values. Expect this step in front of every external destination: AI services, vendor support, MSSPs, and shared data lakes. Benefits of Log Analytics Faster scoping for incident responders. A correlated timeline answers “which hosts, which accounts, since when” in minutes, which drives containment and shortens dwell time. Validated detections for engineers. Replaying logs against rule logic shows which Sigma rules fire, which are noisy, and which ATT&CK techniques have no coverage. Compliance evidence. PCI DSS Requirement 10, ISO/IEC 27001 control A.8.15, and NIS2 all expect security events to be logged and reviewed. Root cause for administrators. The journalctl output that explains a failed service often reveals a misconfiguration an attacker could abuse. Lower SIEM cost. You can analyze a short-lived source once without onboarding it. Safer collaboration. Pseudonymized logs let a retainer, MSSP, or vendor TAC cluster hosts and users without seeing real identities. Use Cases for Log Analytics Unmanaged host triage. A contractor laptop without EDR is suspected of compromise. Export Security, Sysmon, and PowerShell logs and check LogTotal findings for credential access (T1003), PowerShell execution (T1059.001), and scheduled tasks (T1053.005) before reimaging. Cloud account takeover. After an unfamiliar ConsoleLogin, pull 72 hours of CloudTrail and Entra ID sign-ins and look for new access keys, MFA changes, and IAM policy edits. External IR retainers and vendor TAC. Sanitize the evidence with a key you keep. The third party still clusters hosts and users by token, and you map tokens back internally. Detection engineering. Replay Atomic Red Team or Caldera logs to confirm which rules fire, then sanitize the fixtures before they reach Git or CI artifacts. Privacy reviews. Keyed pseudonymization is a documentable technical measure under GDPR Article 32: what was replaced, how tokens were generated, who holds the key. How to Perform Log Analysis: Locate and Export Logs by Platform Every procedure below ends in a format LogTotal reads natively: EVTX, CEF, JSON/NDJSON, or syslog. Fix the UTC time window and scope first, and hash each export (Get-FileHash or sha256sum) for chain of custody. Windows (EVTX). Requires an elevated shell as local Administrator. Live .evtx files under %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\ are locked by the Event Log service, so export them with wevtutil: wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\Security.evtx wevtutil epl “Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational” C:\IR\Sysmon.evtx Add /q:”*[System[TimeCreated[timediff(@SystemTime) <= 86400000]]]” to limit the export to 24 hours. GUI path: eventvwr.msc → Windows Logs → Security → Save All Events As… Linux (syslog or NDJSON). Requires root or membership in adm / systemd-journal. Copy /var/log/auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL). For journald: sudo journalctl –since “2026-10-20” –until “2026-10-21” –utc -o json > host01.ndjson AWS CloudTrail (JSON). From a trail bucket (s3:GetObject, kms:Decrypt), flatten the records into NDJSON: zcat ./ct/*.json.gz | jq -c ‘.Records[]’ > cloudtrail.ndjson Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 (JSON). Entra admin center → Identity → Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs → Download → JSON (Reports Reader role). For Purview audit data, skip the CSV export and pull the JSON directly (Audit Logs role): Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate 2026-10-20 -EndDate 2026-10-21 -ResultSize 5000 | Select-Object -ExpandProperty AuditData | Out-File .\m365.ndjson -Encoding utf8 Network devices (CEF). Switch the device to CEF (on FortiGate: config log syslogd setting → set format cef) and export lines containing CEF:0| from the syslog collector. SOC Prime Offerings for Log Analytics Threat Detection Marketplace : 1,000,000+ Sigma-native detection rules, translated to SIEM, EDR, and data lake languages and tagged with ATT&CK. Prime Hunt : scans historical SIEM, EDR, and data lake data with relevant rules and infers Attack Chains from the results. Prime Detect : runs Sigma rules on streaming events before the SIEM and correlates them into Attack Chains in real time. Uncoder.IO : translates Sigma and Roota rules into native queries. LogTotal : free, no-sign-up analysis of exported log files with in-browser sanitization. logtotal-sanitizer : the Apache 2.0 engine behind LogTotal, as a Node.js library and CLI for on-prem or air-gapped use. LogTotal covers the case this guide is about: a file from a source outside your SIEM, or one you cannot share raw. Each analysis runs on a disposable, dedicated instance of SOC Prime’s DetectFlow engine and is deleted afterward. How Log Analytics with LogTotal Works LogTotal is free, needs no account, and sanitizes files in your browser before anything is uploaded. SOC Prime does not retain logs after analysis or train on them. Open logtotal.com in a current Chromium, Firefox, or Safari build. Load the export. Drop the .evtx, .log, .json, or .ndjson file. The format is detected automatically. Review sanitization. Secrets, cookies, payment IDs, IPs, hostnames, usernames, and home-directory paths become keyed HMAC-SHA-256 tokens such as or . Identical values get identical tokens, so ten sprayed accounts still look like ten users. Download the sanitized copy for your case file. It is exactly what was analyzed. Run the analysis. Events are checked against roughly 1,000,000 detection rules and 13,000 labels, then correlated with Higher-Order Sigma rules and agentic AI. SOC Prime cites up to 1.7 million events in under a minute. Read the findings. Detections are mapped to ATT&CK, grouped into attack chains, and explained by AI. items.summary_html:
What Is Log Analytics?

Log analytics is the practice of collecting, parsing, normalizing, and querying machine-generated event records to answer an operational or security question. In a SOC, that question is usually narrow: did this account authenticate from an unexpected source, did this host spawn an unusual child process, which API calls preceded the data transfer.

The raw material is heterogeneous: Windows Security and Sysmon channels in .evtx files, Linux auth.log and journald output, firewall and proxy events in CEF, and cloud audit trails such as AWS CloudTrail or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs exported as JSON.

A working log analytics pipeline has four stages:

  1. Collection. Export events from the source without losing fields or timestamps.
  2. Normalization. Map src_ip, IpAddress, and sourceIPAddress to one common schema.
  3. Detection. Run Sigma or vendor rules and tag every hit with MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
  4. Correlation. Group related hits into a timeline or attack chain that an analyst can validate.
Why Log Analytics Matters for Detection and Response

Logs are often the only record that survives an intrusion. EDR telemetry rolls over, memory is lost on reboot, and packet capture is rarely running when you need it. Windows Event IDs 4624, 4672, and 4688, or CloudTrail calls such as ConsoleLogin and CreateAccessKey, are typically the primary evidence for scoping an incident.

Three pressures make log analytics a core SOC skill rather than a SIEM feature:

  • Volume. A single incident can produce millions of events, and grep only finds what you already know to look for.
  • Coverage gaps. Contractor laptops, OT segments, and SaaS tenants nobody connected are not in the SIEM, but their logs still need analysis.
  • Data handling. Logs carry usernames, hostnames, IPs, session cookies, and bearer tokens. Under GDPR much of that is personal data, and a leaked token is a live access path.

Every log attached to a vendor ticket or pasted into an AI chat widens the circle of people and jurisdictions that can read the original values. Good log analytics answers the question fast without creating a second incident.

A Short History of Log Analytics

Syslog, written by Eric Allman for Sendmail in the early 1980s, was later standardized in RFC 3164 (2001) and RFC 5424 (2009). For two decades, log analysis meant grep and awk on a central syslog server.

Windows went structured. Windows Vista replaced the legacy .evt format with the XML-based .evtx format and the channel model still used today, and Sysmon (2014) added high-fidelity process and network telemetry.

The mid-2000s brought SIEM. ArcSight, QRadar, and later Splunk made centralized search and correlation a product category, and ArcSight’s CEF is still emitted by most network appliances. The 2010s added open stacks such as ELK and cloud audit trails such as CloudTrail (2013).

In 2017, Sigma gave defenders a vendor-neutral rule format. The same year, SOC Prime began tagging Sigma rules with MITRE ATT&CK techniques and applied the approach to the public NotPetya investigation. ATT&CK mapping has since become a default expectation for detection content.

Where Log Analytics Is Heading

Detection moves upstream. Teams run Sigma rules on streaming events in the pipeline before data reaches the SIEM, cutting storage cost and shrinking mean time to detect from hours to minutes.

Correlation beats single alerts. Isolated low-fidelity matches are noise. Higher-order logic that links techniques across hosts and time windows into attack chains gives analysts something to confirm or close.

AI triage meets data-handling limits. LLMs explain process trees and summarize timelines well, but sending raw telemetry to a model provider raises privacy and contractual questions, and frontier models may refuse security content outright. During the July 2026 HuggingFace incident response, an attempt to send about 17,000 events to frontier models was blocked by guardrails.

Pseudonymization becomes a pipeline stage. Static masking destroys correlation, and plain hashes can be reversed by dictionary guessing. Keyed HMAC tokens keep relationships intact while removing the values. Expect this step in front of every external destination: AI services, vendor support, MSSPs, and shared data lakes.

Benefits of Log Analytics
  • Faster scoping for incident responders. A correlated timeline answers “which hosts, which accounts, since when” in minutes, which drives containment and shortens dwell time.
  • Validated detections for engineers. Replaying logs against rule logic shows which Sigma rules fire, which are noisy, and which ATT&CK techniques have no coverage.
  • Compliance evidence. PCI DSS Requirement 10, ISO/IEC 27001 control A.8.15, and NIS2 all expect security events to be logged and reviewed.
  • Root cause for administrators. The journalctl output that explains a failed service often reveals a misconfiguration an attacker could abuse.
  • Lower SIEM cost. You can analyze a short-lived source once without onboarding it.
  • Safer collaboration. Pseudonymized logs let a retainer, MSSP, or vendor TAC cluster hosts and users without seeing real identities.
Use Cases for Log Analytics

Unmanaged host triage. A contractor laptop without EDR is suspected of compromise. Export Security, Sysmon, and PowerShell logs and check LogTotal findings for credential access (T1003), PowerShell execution (T1059.001), and scheduled tasks (T1053.005) before reimaging.

Cloud account takeover. After an unfamiliar ConsoleLogin, pull 72 hours of CloudTrail and Entra ID sign-ins and look for new access keys, MFA changes, and IAM policy edits.

External IR retainers and vendor TAC. Sanitize the evidence with a key you keep. The third party still clusters hosts and users by token, and you map tokens back internally.

Detection engineering. Replay Atomic Red Team or Caldera logs to confirm which rules fire, then sanitize the fixtures before they reach Git or CI artifacts.

Privacy reviews. Keyed pseudonymization is a documentable technical measure under GDPR Article 32: what was replaced, how tokens were generated, who holds the key.

How to Perform Log Analysis: Locate and Export Logs by Platform

Every procedure below ends in a format LogTotal reads natively: EVTX, CEF, JSON/NDJSON, or syslog. Fix the UTC time window and scope first, and hash each export (Get-FileHash or sha256sum) for chain of custody.

Windows (EVTX). Requires an elevated shell as local Administrator. Live .evtx files under %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\ are locked by the Event Log service, so export them with wevtutil:

wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\Security.evtx

wevtutil epl “Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational” C:\IR\Sysmon.evtx

Add /q:”*[System[TimeCreated[timediff(@SystemTime) <= 86400000]]]” to limit the export to 24 hours. GUI path: eventvwr.msc → Windows Logs → Security → Save All Events As…

Linux (syslog or NDJSON). Requires root or membership in adm / systemd-journal. Copy /var/log/auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL). For journald:

sudo journalctl –since “2026-10-20” –until “2026-10-21” –utc -o json > host01.ndjson

AWS CloudTrail (JSON). Requires cloudtrail:LookupEvents. CloudTrail → Event history → Download events → Download JSON covers 90 days of management events. From a trail bucket (s3:GetObject, kms:Decrypt), flatten the records into NDJSON:

zcat ./ct/*.json.gz | jq -c ‘.Records[]’ > cloudtrail.ndjson

Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 (JSON). Entra admin center → Identity → Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs → Download → JSON (Reports Reader role). For Purview audit data, skip the CSV export and pull the JSON directly (Audit Logs role):

Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate 2026-10-20 -EndDate 2026-10-21 -ResultSize 5000 |

  Select-Object -ExpandProperty AuditData | Out-File .\m365.ndjson -Encoding utf8

Network devices (CEF). Switch the device to CEF (on FortiGate: config log syslogd setting → set format cef) and export lines containing CEF:0| from the syslog collector.

SOC Prime Offerings for Log Analytics
  • Threat Detection Marketplace: 1,000,000+ Sigma-native detection rules, translated to SIEM, EDR, and data lake languages and tagged with ATT&CK.
  • Prime Hunt: scans historical SIEM, EDR, and data lake data with relevant rules and infers Attack Chains from the results.
  • Prime Detect: runs Sigma rules on streaming events before the SIEM and correlates them into Attack Chains in real time.
  • Uncoder.IO: translates Sigma and Roota rules into native queries.
  • LogTotal: free, no-sign-up analysis of exported log files with in-browser sanitization.
  • logtotal-sanitizer: the Apache 2.0 engine behind LogTotal, as a Node.js library and CLI for on-prem or air-gapped use.

LogTotal covers the case this guide is about: a file from a source outside your SIEM, or one you cannot share raw. Each analysis runs on a disposable, dedicated instance of SOC Prime’s DetectFlow engine and is deleted afterward.

How Log Analytics with LogTotal Works

LogTotal is free, needs no account, and sanitizes files in your browser before anything is uploaded. SOC Prime does not retain logs after analysis or train on them.

  1. Open logtotal.com in a current Chromium, Firefox, or Safari build.
  2. Load the export. Drop the .evtx, .log, .json, or .ndjson file. The format is detected automatically.
  3. Review sanitization. Secrets, cookies, payment IDs, IPs, hostnames, usernames, and home-directory paths become keyed HMAC-SHA-256 tokens such as or . Identical values get identical tokens, so ten sprayed accounts still look like ten users.
  4. Download the sanitized copy for your case file. It is exactly what was analyzed.
  5. Run the analysis. Events are checked against roughly 1,000,000 detection rules and 13,000 labels, then correlated with Higher-Order Sigma rules and agentic AI. SOC Prime cites up to 1.7 million events in under a minute.
  6. Read the findings. Detections are mapped to ATT&CK, grouped into attack chains, and explained by AI. A token that appears in both credential-access and lateral-movement findings is your account to reset.

For several hosts, or when browser uploads are off-limits, sanitize locally with the open-source CLI (Node.js 20+) and reuse one key so tokens match across files:

npm install -g @socprime/logtotal-sanitizer

logtotal-sanitize ./dc01.log -o ./dc01.sanitized.log –print-key

logtotal-sanitize ./ws17.log -o ./ws17.sanitized.log –key “$KEY”

FAQ

Which log formats does LogTotal accept?

EVTX, CEF, JSON/NDJSON, and syslog, detected automatically. Convert CSV exports to NDJSON first.

Do my raw logs leave my machine?

No. Sanitization runs in the browser, analysis runs on a disposable instance, and nothing is retained. For stricter policies, run the sanitizer on-prem or air-gapped.

How many events can one analysis handle?

SOC Prime cites up to 1.7 million events. Split larger cases by host or time window and sanitize every slice with the same key.

Can I map a token back to the real value?

Only with your key: recompute the HMAC for a known value and compare. Without the key, tokens resist dictionary guessing.

( + KQL Queries) Two critical vulnerabilities affecting PHP have been disclosed ahead of their scheduled security release. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619 and commonly referred to as PHP2Shell, have received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 from the PHP security team. An emergency security release is scheduled for October 21, 2026, at 14:00 UTC. At the time of writing, the official affected version ranges and complete technical details have not yet been published. Initial reports suggest that older PHP versions may also be affected. Without confirmed exploitation details, that would be premature. Instead, we can identify PHP installations, investigate suspicious process execution, review network connections, and establish a baseline of PHP-related activity. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management provides software inventory information through the DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory table. One important detail: searching for every software name containing php will also return PHP libraries and packages such as php-json, php-symfony or php-psr-http-message. Their software versions are not PHP runtime versions. For this reason, I prefer to start with packages that are more likely to represent the PHP interpreter. DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where SoftwareName matches regex @"(?i)^php([0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?)?(_for_linux)?$" or SoftwareName matches regex @"(?i)^php[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?-(cli|fpm|cgi|common)$" | extend VersionFromName = extract(@"(?i)^php([0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?)", 1, SoftwareName) | extend VersionFromPackage = extract(@"^(?:\d+:)?(\d+\.\d+(?:\.\d+)?)", 1, SoftwareVersion) | extend PHPVersion = iff( isnotempty(VersionFromName), VersionFromName, VersionFromPackage ) | extend Major = toint(split(PHPVersion, ".")[0]), Minor = toint(split(PHPVersion, ".")[1]) | extend Priority = case( Major < 8, "Legacy PHP", Major == 8 and Minor <= 1, "End of Life", Major == 8 and Minor >= 2, "Verify security updates", "Unknown" ) | summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 100) by SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, PHPVersion, Priority | order by Devices desc This query helps identify legacy installations and prioritize further investigation. Keep in mind that software inventory is not always complete. PHP can also be bundled with third-party applications, installed in containers, or deployed outside standard package managers. Additionally, Linux distributions may backport security fixes without changing the upstream PHP version. The version alone does not always tell the complete story. 2. PHP spawning suspicious processes One of the first things I would investigate is PHP or web server processes spawning operating system commands. Under normal circumstances, depending on the application, a PHP worker may not need to launch shells or system utilities. Examples worth investigating include: php-fpm → sh apache2 → bash php-cgi.exe → cmd.exe w3wp.exe → powershell.exe httpd → curl We can investigate these relationships using DeviceProcessEvents: let WebProcesses = dynamic([ "php", "php.exe", "php-cgi", "php-cgi.exe", "php-fpm", "apache2", "httpd", "nginx", "w3wp.exe" ]); let SuspiciousProcesses = dynamic([ "sh", "bash", "dash", "zsh", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "curl", "curl.exe", "wget", "python", "python3", "python.exe", "perl", "nc", "ncat", "socat", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe" ]); DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcesses) or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm" | where FileName in~ (SuspiciousProcesses) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA1 | order by Timestamp desc The interesting part is the relationship between the parent process and the child process. Finding bash or curl on a Linux server is not particularly interesting. Finding bash launched by a PHP worker handling external requests deserves more attention. Of course, legitimate applications can execute system commands. Results should be reviewed against the application’s expected behavior. Also, not every PHP-FPM or web server process will have one of these exact names. The query may need to be adapted to the environment. 3. Looking for reconnaissance command After obtaining command execution on a server, attackers may try to understand the environment. Common commands include: whoami , id , uname , hostname , ipconfig , ifconfig and systeminfo . Rather than searching for these commands across every process, we can focus on processes started by PHP or web server components. DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ( "php", "apache", "httpd", "nginx", "w3wp" ) | where FileName in~ ( "whoami", "whoami.exe", "id", "uname", "hostname", "hostname.exe", "ifconfig", "ipconfig.exe", "systeminfo.exe" ) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc This is a relatively simple query, but it can help identify early post-exploitation activity. The parent-process filter is important. Running whoami from an interactive administrative shell is different from running it through a web server process. 4. PHP creating files in suspicious locations Another behavior worth investigating is PHP creating files in temporary directories or web application folders. Huntress recently documented a separate PHP abuse case involving temporary PHP files that were created, executed and subsequently removed. That incident was not attributed to PHP2Shell, but the behavior is relevant when investigating possible web application compromise. Using DeviceFileEvents, we can look for PHP files created or modified by web-related processes: DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType in~ ( "FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed" ) | where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" | where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ( "php", "apache", "httpd", "nginx", "w3wp" ) | where FolderPath contains "/tmp/" or FolderPath contains "/var/tmp/" or FolderPath contains "/dev/shm/" or FolderPath contains "/var/www/" or FolderPath contains "wwwroot" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA1 | order by Timestamp desc A PHP file created in a web directory is not necessarily malicious. However, unexpected file creation by a web server process, particularly in a temporary directory, is worth investigating. For more advanced analysis, I would also look at files created and deleted within a short period of time. That can help identify temporary payload execution. 5. Investigating outbound network connections If an attacker obtains code execution through a vulnerable PHP application, one possible next step is establishing an outbound connection. This could involve downloading additional payloads, contacting external infrastructure or establishing a reverse shell. Using DeviceNetworkEvents, we can identify outbound connections initiated by PHP and web server processes. let WebProcesses = dynamic([ "php", "php.exe", "php-cgi", "php-cgi.exe", "php-fpm", "apache2", "httpd", "nginx", "w3wp.exe" ]); DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess" | where RemoteIPType == "Public" | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcesses) or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm" | summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 30), URLs = make_set(RemoteUrl, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP | order by Connections asc Here I would pay particular attention to destinations that are rarely contacted, unusual ports and connections that occur shortly after suspicious process execution. One limitation is that some PHP applications legitimately communicate with external APIs, payment gateways, update services and other Internet resources. 6. Finding new child processes: PHP execution baseline This is probably the hunting approach I find most interesting. Instead of looking only for a predefined list of suspicious executables, we can compare recent PHP-related process execution with historical activity. For example, suppose a PHP server has been running for several weeks and has never launched python3. Suddenly, php-fpm starts executing python3. That does not automatically mean compromise, but it is a change worth reviewing. We can use a 28-day baseline and compare it against the last two days. let WebProcesses = dynamic([ "php", "php.exe", "php-cgi", "php-cgi.exe", "php-fpm", "apache2", "httpd", "nginx", "w3wp.exe" ]); let Baseline = DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(2d)) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcesses) or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm" | distinct DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName; DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(2d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcesses) or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm" | join kind=leftanti Baseline on DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName | summarize Executions = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Commands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName | order by Executions asc This approach is not specific to PHP2Shell. It can also help identify unexpected behavior resulting from other web application vulnerabilities. There are some limitations: the historical baseline depends on telemetry retention, endpoint coverage and the stability of the application. New deployments and legitimate maintenance activities can introduce new process relationships. Still, comparing behavior before and after a vulnerability disclosure is something I find useful during threat hunting investigations. 7. What about HTTP requests and web server logs? Endpoint telemetry is only one part of the investigation. If Apache, Nginx, IIS or WAF logs are available in Microsoft Sentinel, I would also investigate: Unusual HTTP POST requests targeting PHP applications. Repeated HTTP 5xx responses from the same source. Unexpected PHP worker crashes or restarts. Suspicious HTTP requests followed by new process execution. Changes in request volume or behavior around the disclosure date. Some preliminary technical discussions mention multipart requests and PHP session upload handling. However, until the technical details are officially confirmed, I would treat these as research leads rather than validated exploitation indicators. For me, the most useful investigation would be correlating an unusual HTTP request with subsequent process execution or network activity on the same server. The exact KQL will depend on the web server and WAF log schema being ingested into Sentinel. Final notes These queries are starting points for threat hunting in Microsoft Defender XDR, not validated detections for CVE-2026–109618 or CVE-2026–109619. They depend on endpoint telemetry being available, particularly on Linux servers where PHP is commonly deployed. I would start by identifying PHP installations, prioritizing Internet-facing servers, and reviewing unexpected process execution. For unsupported PHP versions, upgrading or restricting exposure should be considered while the affected versions and available patches are confirmed. items.summary_html:
🚨 PHP2Shell: Two Critical PHP Vulnerabilities (CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619) — Are Your Servers Ready? ( + KQL Queries)

Two critical vulnerabilities affecting PHP have been disclosed ahead of their scheduled security release.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619 and commonly referred to as PHP2Shell, have received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 from the PHP security team.

An emergency security release is scheduled for October 21, 2026, at 14:00 UTC. At the time of writing, the official affected version ranges and complete technical details have not yet been published. Initial reports suggest that older PHP versions may also be affected.

While waiting for the official advisory, I wanted to explore what we can already investigate using Microsoft Defender XDR and KQL. The objective is not to detect these two vulnerabilities directly. Without confirmed exploitation details, that would be premature. Instead, we can identify PHP installations, investigate suspicious process execution, review network connections, and establish a baseline of PHP-related activity.

Here are a few hunting queries worth exploring.

1. Identifying PHP installations and versions

Before investigating potential exploitation, we need to understand where PHP is installed. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management provides software inventory information through the DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory table.

One important detail: searching for every software name containing php will also return PHP libraries and packages such as php-json, php-symfony or php-psr-http-message. Their software versions are not PHP runtime versions.

For this reason, I prefer to start with packages that are more likely to represent the PHP interpreter.

DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName matches regex
    @"(?i)^php([0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?)?(_for_linux)?$"
    or SoftwareName matches regex
    @"(?i)^php[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?-(cli|fpm|cgi|common)$"
| extend VersionFromName =
    extract(@"(?i)^php([0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?)",
        1, SoftwareName)
| extend VersionFromPackage =
    extract(@"^(?:\d+:)?(\d+\.\d+(?:\.\d+)?)",
        1, SoftwareVersion)
| extend PHPVersion = iff(
    isnotempty(VersionFromName),
    VersionFromName,
    VersionFromPackage
)
| extend Major = toint(split(PHPVersion, ".")[0]),
         Minor = toint(split(PHPVersion, ".")[1])
| extend Priority = case(
    Major < 8, "Legacy PHP",
    Major == 8 and Minor <= 1, "End of Life",
    Major == 8 and Minor >= 2, "Verify security updates",
    "Unknown"
)
| summarize
    Devices = dcount(DeviceId),
    DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 100)
    by SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
       PHPVersion, Priority
| order by Devices desc

This query helps identify legacy installations and prioritize further investigation. Keep in mind that software inventory is not always complete. PHP can also be bundled with third-party applications, installed in containers, or deployed outside standard package managers. Additionally, Linux distributions may backport security fixes without changing the upstream PHP version. The version alone does not always tell the complete story.

2. PHP spawning suspicious processes

One of the first things I would investigate is PHP or web server processes spawning operating system commands. Under normal circumstances, depending on the application, a PHP worker may not need to launch shells or system utilities. Examples worth investigating include:

  • php-fpm → sh
  • apache2 → bash
  • php-cgi.exe → cmd.exe
  • w3wp.exe → powershell.exe
  • httpd → curl

We can investigate these relationships using DeviceProcessEvents:

let WebProcesses = dynamic([
    "php", "php.exe",
    "php-cgi", "php-cgi.exe",
    "php-fpm",
    "apache2", "httpd",
    "nginx", "w3wp.exe"
]);
let SuspiciousProcesses = dynamic([
    "sh", "bash", "dash", "zsh",
    "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe",
    "curl", "curl.exe", "wget",
    "python", "python3", "python.exe",
    "perl", "nc", "ncat", "socat",
    "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe"
]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcesses)
    or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm"
| where FileName in~ (SuspiciousProcesses)
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine,
    FolderPath,
    SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc

The interesting part is the relationship between the parent process and the child process.

Finding bash or curl on a Linux server is not particularly interesting. Finding bash launched by a PHP worker handling external requests deserves more attention. Of course, legitimate applications can execute system commands. Results should be reviewed against the application’s expected behavior. Also, not every PHP-FPM or web server process will have one of these exact names. The query may need to be adapted to the environment.

3. Looking for reconnaissance command

After obtaining command execution on a server, attackers may try to understand the environment. Common commands include:

whoami, id, uname, hostname, ipconfig, ifconfig and systeminfo.

Rather than searching for these commands across every process, we can focus on processes started by PHP or web server components.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (
    "php", "apache", "httpd", "nginx", "w3wp"
)
| where FileName in~ (
    "whoami", "whoami.exe",
    "id", "uname", "hostname", "hostname.exe",
    "ifconfig", "ipconfig.exe",
    "systeminfo.exe"
)
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

This is a relatively simple query, but it can help identify early post-exploitation activity. The parent-process filter is important. Running whoami from an interactive administrative shell is different from running it through a web server process.

4. PHP creating files in suspicious locations

Another behavior worth investigating is PHP creating files in temporary directories or web application folders. Huntress recently documented a separate PHP abuse case involving temporary PHP files that were created, executed and subsequently removed. That incident was not attributed to PHP2Shell, but the behavior is relevant when investigating possible web application compromise. Using DeviceFileEvents, we can look for PHP files created or modified by web-related processes:

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in~ (
    "FileCreated",
    "FileModified",
    "FileRenamed"
)
| where FileName endswith ".php"
    or FileName endswith ".phtml"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (
    "php", "apache", "httpd", "nginx", "w3wp"
)
| where FolderPath contains "/tmp/"
    or FolderPath contains "/var/tmp/"
    or FolderPath contains "/dev/shm/"
    or FolderPath contains "/var/www/"
    or FolderPath contains "wwwroot"
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    ActionType,
    FileName,
    FolderPath,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
A PHP file created in a web directory is not necessarily malicious. However, unexpected file creation by a web server process, particularly in a temporary directory, is worth investigating.

For more advanced analysis, I would also look at files created and deleted within a short period of time. That can help identify temporary payload execution.

5. Investigating outbound network connections

If an attacker obtains code execution through a vulnerable PHP application, one possible next step is establishing an outbound connection. This could involve downloading additional payloads, contacting external infrastructure or establishing a reverse shell.

Using DeviceNetworkEvents, we can identify outbound connections initiated by PHP and web server processes.

let WebProcesses = dynamic([
    "php", "php.exe",
    "php-cgi", "php-cgi.exe",
    "php-fpm",
    "apache2", "httpd",
    "nginx", "w3wp.exe"
]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcesses)
    or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm"
| summarize
    Connections = count(),
    FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
    LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
    Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 30),
    URLs = make_set(RemoteUrl, 20)
    by DeviceName,
       InitiatingProcessFileName,
       InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
       RemoteIP
| order by Connections asc

Here I would pay particular attention to destinations that are rarely contacted, unusual ports and connections that occur shortly after suspicious process execution. One limitation is that some PHP applications legitimately communicate with external APIs, payment gateways, update services and other Internet resources.

6. Finding new child processes: PHP execution baseline

This is probably the hunting approach I find most interesting. Instead of looking only for a predefined list of suspicious executables, we can compare recent PHP-related process execution with historical activity.

For example, suppose a PHP server has been running for several weeks and has never launched python3. Suddenly, php-fpm starts executing python3. That does not automatically mean compromise, but it is a change worth reviewing. We can use a 28-day baseline and compare it against the last two days.

let WebProcesses = dynamic([
    "php", "php.exe",
    "php-cgi", "php-cgi.exe",
    "php-fpm",
    "apache2", "httpd",
    "nginx", "w3wp.exe"
]);
let Baseline =
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(2d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcesses)
        or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm"
    | distinct
        DeviceId,
        InitiatingProcessFileName,
        FileName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(2d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcesses)
    or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline
    on DeviceId,
       InitiatingProcessFileName,
       FileName
| summarize
    Executions = count(),
    FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
    LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
    Commands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10)
    by DeviceName,
       InitiatingProcessFileName,
       FileName
| order by Executions asc

This approach is not specific to PHP2Shell. It can also help identify unexpected behavior resulting from other web application vulnerabilities. There are some limitations: the historical baseline depends on telemetry retention, endpoint coverage and the stability of the application. New deployments and legitimate maintenance activities can introduce new process relationships. Still, comparing behavior before and after a vulnerability disclosure is something I find useful during threat hunting investigations.

7. What about HTTP requests and web server logs?

Endpoint telemetry is only one part of the investigation. If Apache, Nginx, IIS or WAF logs are available in Microsoft Sentinel, I would also investigate:

  • Unusual HTTP POST requests targeting PHP applications.
  • Repeated HTTP 5xx responses from the same source.
  • Unexpected PHP worker crashes or restarts.
  • Suspicious HTTP requests followed by new process execution.
  • Changes in request volume or behavior around the disclosure date.

Some preliminary technical discussions mention multipart requests and PHP session upload handling. However, until the technical details are officially confirmed, I would treat these as research leads rather than validated exploitation indicators.

For me, the most useful investigation would be correlating an unusual HTTP request with subsequent process execution or network activity on the same server.

The exact KQL will depend on the web server and WAF log schema being ingested into Sentinel.

Final notes

These queries are starting points for threat hunting in Microsoft Defender XDR, not validated detections for CVE-2026–109618 or CVE-2026–109619. They depend on endpoint telemetry being available, particularly on Linux servers where PHP is commonly deployed.

I would start by identifying PHP installations, prioritizing Internet-facing servers, and reviewing unexpected process execution. For unsupported PHP versions, upgrading or restricting exposure should be considered while the affected versions and available patches are confirmed.

References
  • Huntress — PHP2Shell: Leaked Critical PHP Vulnerabilities
  • PHP Official Website
  • CERT-EU — Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP

How to Export Windows Event Logs (EVTX)
items.summary: The short answer: open Event Viewer, right-click the log you need (for example Windows Logs → Security ), choose Save All Events As… , and keep the .evtx format. From an elevated command prompt, the same thing is one line: wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\security.evtx. Don’t copy the files out of C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs with Explorer. The Event Log service keeps them open, so you usually get an error or nothing usable. EVTX is worth the extra minute compared with a text export. It’s the native format, so every field, the record IDs and the exact UTC timestamps survive. A SIEM can’t give you that back, because it stores rendered text. Prime Core has 11,632 sigma rules for Windows event logs, mapped to 643 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. They range from password guessing (T1110) and malicious services (T1543.003) to attackers clearing the logs behind them (T1070.001). Below is how to export the right logs, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Try LogTotal, free TL;DR Route Use it when What you need Event Viewer → Save All Events As One machine, one or two logs, you have a desktop session Admin rights, or Event Log Readers for most logs wevtutil epl You want a filtered export, a script, or a server without a GUI An elevated prompt wevtutil with /r: or a PowerShell loop Several logs, or a remote machine Admin rights on the target, plus remote event log access through the firewall Before you start Three things decide whether the export contains what you hope it contains. Rights. Administrators can export any log. Members of the local Event Log Readers group can read most logs without full admin. For the Security log, an elevated prompt is the dependable choice. Details are in our [Windows event log permissions guide]. Audit policy. Windows only logs what it’s told to. Process creation (event 4688) isn’t audited by default. Even when it is, the command line is recorded only if a separate policy is enabled. Check before you go looking for events that were never written: auditpol /get /category:* Log size and overwrite. Every log has a maximum size. By default, Windows overwrites the oldest events once the log is full, and on a busy server or domain controller that can mean only hours of history. See what you’re working with: wevtutil gl Security Look at maxSize and retention. If the attack happened before the oldest event in the log, it isn’t in there. Check your SIEM or forwarded events instead. And the usual reminder: event logs are full of usernames, hostnames and IPs. LogTotal sanitizes uploads, but your data-handling policy still applies. Which logs to export “The Windows logs” is a few hundred channels on a modern system. For security work, these are the ones that usually carry the story: Log (channel name) What it gives you Notes Security Logons (4624, 4625), account changes (4720, 4728), log cleared (1102), process creation (4688) 4688 only if auditing is on System New services (7045), service changes (7036), System log cleared (104) Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational Process creation with hashes and command lines, network connections, and more Only if Sysmon is installed Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational Script block logging (4104), the actual code that ran Only if script block logging is enabled Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational Detections (1116) and actions taken (1117) Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational New scheduled tasks (106), a favorite persistence trick Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational RDP session logon, disconnect, reconnect (21, 24, 25) Not sure what a machine has? wevtutil el lists every channel. Pipe it through findstr /i sysmon (or whatever you’re hunting for) to check a specific one. Option 1: Event Viewer Best for one machine and a couple of logs. Press Win+R, type eventvwr.msc, and run it as administrator. Find the log. The classic ones are under Windows Logs . Everything else lives under Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows . Sysmon, for example, is at …\Windows\Sysmon\Operational. Right-click the log and choose Save All Events As… Keep Event Files (*.evtx) as the type and give the file a name that says what it is, like dc-01_security_2026-10-20.evtx. Windows then asks about display information. That decides whether a LocaleMetaData folder with message text gets saved next to the file, which helps when someone opens it in Event Viewer on another machine. For a LogTotal upload, the .evtx file is what counts. Need only part of the log? Use Filter Current Log… first (event IDs, time range), then Save Filtered Log File As… . The XML tab of that filter dialog shows the exact XPath query it built. Copy it; you’ll want it for wevtutil in a minute. Option 2: wevtutil from the command line wevtutil ships with every Windows version you’re likely to meet. It works without a GUI and can filter while it exports. Run it from an elevated prompt. The whole log: mkdir C:\logs wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\dc-01_security.evtx Only the last 24 hours (the number is milliseconds): wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\dc-01_security_24h.evtx /q:”*[System[TimeCreated[timediff(@SystemTime) <= 86400000]]]” An exact window, in UTC: wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\dc-01_security_1019.evtx /q:”*[System[TimeCreated[@SystemTime>=’2026-10-19T00:00:00.000Z’ and @SystemTime<‘2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z’]]]” Only logons, successful and failed: wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\dc-01_logons.evtx /q:”*[System[(EventID=4624 or EventID=4625)]]” Channel names with spaces need quotes: wevtutil epl “Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational” C:\logs\defender.evtx If the target file already exists, wevtutil refuses to overwrite it unless you add /ow:true. items.summary_html:
The short answer: open Event Viewer, right-click the log you need (for example Windows Logs → Security), choose Save All Events As…, and keep the .evtx format. From an elevated command prompt, the same thing is one line: wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\security.evtx. Don’t copy the files out of C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs with Explorer. The Event Log service keeps them open, so you usually get an error or nothing usable.

EVTX is worth the extra minute compared with a text export. It’s the native format, so every field, the record IDs and the exact UTC timestamps survive. A SIEM can’t give you that back, because it stores rendered text. Prime Core has 11,632 sigma rules for Windows event logs, mapped to 643 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. They range from password guessing (T1110) and malicious services (T1543.003) to attackers clearing the logs behind them (T1070.001). Below is how to export the right logs, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Try LogTotal, free

TL;DR

RouteUse it whenWhat you needEvent Viewer → Save All Events AsOne machine, one or two logs, you have a desktop sessionAdmin rights, or Event Log Readers for most logswevtutil eplYou want a filtered export, a script, or a server without a GUIAn elevated promptwevtutil with /r: or a PowerShell loopSeveral logs, or a remote machineAdmin rights on the target, plus remote event log access through the firewall Before you start

Three things decide whether the export contains what you hope it contains.

Rights. Administrators can export any log. Members of the local Event Log Readers group can read most logs without full admin. For the Security log, an elevated prompt is the dependable choice. Details are in our [Windows event log permissions guide].

Audit policy. Windows only logs what it’s told to. Process creation (event 4688) isn’t audited by default. Even when it is, the command line is recorded only if a separate policy is enabled. Check before you go looking for events that were never written:

auditpol /get /category:*

Log size and overwrite. Every log has a maximum size. By default, Windows overwrites the oldest events once the log is full, and on a busy server or domain controller that can mean only hours of history. See what you’re working with:

wevtutil gl Security

Look at maxSize and retention. If the attack happened before the oldest event in the log, it isn’t in there. Check your SIEM or forwarded events instead.

And the usual reminder: event logs are full of usernames, hostnames and IPs. LogTotal sanitizes uploads, but your data-handling policy still applies.

Which logs to export

“The Windows logs” is a few hundred channels on a modern system. For security work, these are the ones that usually carry the story:

Log (channel name)What it gives youNotesSecurityLogons (4624, 4625), account changes (4720, 4728), log cleared (1102), process creation (4688)4688 only if auditing is onSystemNew services (7045), service changes (7036), System log cleared (104)Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/OperationalProcess creation with hashes and command lines, network connections, and moreOnly if Sysmon is installedMicrosoft-Windows-PowerShell/OperationalScript block logging (4104), the actual code that ranOnly if script block logging is enabledMicrosoft-Windows-Windows Defender/OperationalDetections (1116) and actions taken (1117)Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/OperationalNew scheduled tasks (106), a favorite persistence trickMicrosoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/OperationalRDP session logon, disconnect, reconnect (21, 24, 25)

Not sure what a machine has? wevtutil el lists every channel. Pipe it through findstr /i sysmon (or whatever you’re hunting for) to check a specific one.

Option 1: Event Viewer

Best for one machine and a couple of logs.

  1. Press Win+R, type eventvwr.msc, and run it as administrator.
  2. Find the log. The classic ones are under Windows Logs. Everything else lives under Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows. Sysmon, for example, is at …\Windows\Sysmon\Operational.
  3. Right-click the log and choose Save All Events As…
  4. Keep Event Files (*.evtx) as the type and give the file a name that says what it is, like dc-01_security_2026-10-20.evtx.
  5. Windows then asks about display information. That decides whether a LocaleMetaData folder with message text gets saved next to the file, which helps when someone opens it in Event Viewer on another machine. For a LogTotal upload, the .evtx file is what counts.

Need only part of the log? Use Filter Current Log… first (event IDs, time range), then Save Filtered Log File As…. The XML tab of that filter dialog shows the exact XPath query it built. Copy it; you’ll want it for wevtutil in a minute.

Option 2: wevtutil from the command line

wevtutil ships with every Windows version you’re likely to meet. It works without a GUI and can filter while it exports. Run it from an elevated prompt.

The whole log:

mkdir C:\logs
wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\dc-01_security.evtx

Only the last 24 hours (the number is milliseconds):

wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\dc-01_security_24h.evtx /q:”*[System[TimeCreated[timediff(@SystemTime) <= 86400000]]]”

An exact window, in UTC:

wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\dc-01_security_1019.evtx /q:”*[System[TimeCreated[@SystemTime>=’2026-10-19T00:00:00.000Z’ and @SystemTime<‘2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z’]]]”

Only logons, successful and failed:

wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\dc-01_logons.evtx /q:”*[System[(EventID=4624 or EventID=4625)]]”

Channel names with spaces need quotes:

wevtutil epl “Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational” C:\logs\defender.evtx

If the target file already exists, wevtutil refuses to overwrite it unless you add /ow:true. Writing XPath by hand gets old quickly. Build the filter in Event Viewer and copy the query from the XML tab, as described above.

On a domain controller, filter. An unfiltered Security export from a busy DC can run to gigabytes, and you’ll be uploading most of it for nothing.

Option 3: Several logs, or a remote machine

For triage, you usually want the same handful of logs from every host. This PowerShell snippet exports them into one folder per machine and skips any channel that doesn’t exist (no Sysmon, for example) instead of failing:

$out = “C:\logs\$env:COMPUTERNAME”
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $out | Out-Null

$logs = ‘Security’, ‘System’,
        ‘Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational’,
        ‘Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational’,
        ‘Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational’,
        ‘Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational’

foreach ($l in $logs) {
    $file = Join-Path $out (($l -replace ‘[\\/ ]’, ‘_’) + ‘.evtx’)
    wevtutil epl $l $file /ow:true 2>$null
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { Write-Warning “Skipped: $l” }
}

Remote machines. wevtutil accepts /r:, but there’s a catch people find the hard way: the export file is written on the remote machine’s disk, not yours. Plan to fetch it afterwards:

wevtutil epl Security C:\logs\srv-01_security.evtx /r:srv-01
copy \\srv-01\C$\logs\srv-01_security.evtx .

That needs admin rights on the target and the Remote Event Log Management firewall rules enabled there. If those rules are off and you’d rather not touch them, PowerShell remoting does the same job: run the snippet above through Invoke-Command, then pull the files back with Copy-Item -FromSession.

Upload and review in LogTotal

LogTotal reads EVTX natively, so there’s nothing to convert. It’s SOC Prime’s free service for running detection logic against a log file without setting anything up. 

  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .evtx file. [PROOF: upload screen, size limit, whether several files can go in at once]
  2. Review. [PROOF: what the results screen shows and how findings map to rules and ATT&CK techniques]

What this looks like on real data. We used [PROOF: sample source, e.g. a Security.evtx from a throwaway Windows VM after a simulated attack chain: failed logons, a new local admin, a new service, then the Application log being cleared]. The file was [PROOF: N events, X MB]. LogTotal flagged [PROOF: actual findings, matched rules, ATT&CK techniques].

Want to try it first? [PROOF: link to the sample file] is the same file we used above.

When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFixAccess is deniedPrompt isn’t elevated, or the account lacks rights to that logRun as administratorThe specified channel could not be foundTypo in the channel name, or the component isn’t installed (Sysmon is the usual one)Check with wevtutil el | findstr /i wevtutil complains that the file existsIt doesn’t overwrite by defaultAdd /ow:true, or pick a new file nameThe specified query is invalidXPath quoting or syntaxBuild the filter in Event Viewer and copy it from the XML tabCopying from winevt\Logs fails with “in use by another process”The Event Log service holds the live files openExport with Event Viewer or wevtutil insteadNo 4625 or 4688 events at allThat category isn’t auditedCheck auditpol /get /category:*; this fixes future events, not past onesThe log only goes back a few hoursLog is full and overwritingCheck wevtutil gl Security; look for Archive-Security-*.evtx files if archiving is onThe RPC server is unavailable with /r:Remote Event Log Management firewall rules are offEnable them on the target, or use PowerShell remotingRemote export “succeeded,” but there’s no file/r: writes the file on the remote machineLook on the target’s disk, e.g. \\srv-01\C$\logs
FAQ

Where are EVTX files stored on disk?

In C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs, one file per channel. Channel names with slashes are encoded in the file name, so Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational becomes Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon%4Operational.evtx. You can read the folder, but export through Event Viewer or wevtutil instead of copying the live files.

Can I get logs off a machine that won’t boot?

Yes, and this is the one case where copying works. Mount the disk on another system, or boot from external media. With Windows not running, nothing holds the files open, and you can copy them straight out of Windows\System32\winevt\Logs.

Should I save as EVTX or as XML or text?

EVTX. Event Viewer offers other formats, but they drop structure or bloat the file. EVTX keeps every field and is what LogTotal reads natively.

How far back do my logs go?

As far as the maximum log size allows, and not a day longer. wevtutil gl shows the size and retention settings. In Event Viewer, sort by date and look at the oldest event. If that’s too recent to be useful, raise the size for next time, or better, forward events to a SIEM.

Is it safe to upload event logs to an online tool?

LogTotal sanitizes uploads before analysis and doesn’t retain files.

items.title: Signal bug could let someone keep listening after you hang up
items.summary: A recently disclosed flaw in Signal’s calling software could allow another participant to keep hearing you after you hang up. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-113380 ( CVSS score 9.3 out of 10), affects RingRTC versions earlier than 2.72.0. RingRTC is the open-source library behind Signal’s voice and video calling functionality, providing calling components for its mobile and desktop applications. The flaw concerns how Signal’s calling library shuts down a call. It does not affect how it encrypts conversations. According to the published vulnerability description , another participant could overwhelm a call’s internal event queue and interfere with the steps that should disconnect it when you end the call. The main concern is unwanted listening after someone believes a conversation has ended. If a malicious call participant successfully triggered the flaw, they could potentially continue hearing audio that the other person no longer intended to share. That might include an offhand remark, a conversation with someone nearby, or other private background sound. The vulnerability description also mentions that video might remain active, but does not confirm that behavior or explain what affected users would see on screen. It also doesn’t specify how long any continued transmission might last. There are no known reports of exploitation in the wild. The vulnerability concerns only how a call is shut down. It does not involve stolen passwords, compromised accounts, or exposed message histories that would call for a password reset. What to do The developers updated the code to make shutdown more resilient when a call’s internal queue is full or another termination step fails. Install any available Signal updates on your devices. The fix is available in the underlying RingRTC library, but the affected and first-fixed Signal app versions have not yet been confirmed publicly in the sources reviewed. Personally, I found an update in the Google Play Store which brought my Android app to version 8.32.2. I did not find one in the Apple App Store, although this might be because I have automatic updates enabled . The current version on my iPad is listed as 8.32 (1910). While I think that means it’s all patched, this is hard to confirm from Signal’s website. I’ve emailed Signal for clarification and will update this article when I hear back.
